chapter.title: Passing Props
chapter.description: How data flows from parent to child, and why props cannot be changed by the child.

blocks.text: **Props** are the inputs to a component. A parent passes them as JSX attributes; the child receives them as a single object argument.
Destructuring in the parameter list
Almost all React code destructures props in the function signature. It documents what a component needs at a glance.
Default values
Give a prop a default in the destructuring pattern. The default applies when the prop is missing or explicitly `undefined`.
Props are read only

A component must never modify the props it receives. React relies on components being predictable: the same props should always produce the same output. Mutating props breaks that guarantee and the bug usually shows up somewhere else entirely.
If a child needs to change something, the parent owns that value in state and passes down a function the child can call. Data flows down; events flow up.

blocks.caption: The child asks; the parent decides.

blocks.text: A component is a function that returns UI. That is the whole definition, but the interesting question is where one component should end and the next should begin.
A useful rule of thumb
Give a component one job. If you can describe what it does without using the word 'and', it is probably the right size.

items: `ProductCardAndCheckoutForm` shows a product **and** collects payment. Split it.
`Avatar` shows a user image. Good, and it will be reused everywhere.

blocks.caption: Three small components compose into a list.

blocks.text: Components nest, they do not define

Compose components by rendering them inside each other. Never declare one component inside another component's body: React sees a brand new function type on every render, throws away the old DOM and remounts the subtree, losing its state.
Nested component definitions are a classic cause of 'my input keeps losing focus' and 'my state resets for no reason'. Move the inner component out to the module level.

blocks.text: Anything you put between a component's opening and closing tags arrives as a prop named `children`. This is what makes React components composable.
Composition beats configuration
When a component grows a long list of boolean props, that is usually a sign it should accept content instead of options.

blocks.code:
// Configuration: every new variation needs another prop
<Dialog
  hasHeader
  hasFooter
  showCloseButton
  footerButtonLabel="Save"
/>

// Composition: the caller supplies whatever it needs
<Dialog>
  <Dialog.Header>Edit profile</Dialog.Header>
  <Dialog.Body><ProfileForm /></Dialog.Body>
  <Dialog.Footer><button>Save</button></Dialog.Footer>
</Dialog>

blocks.text: Multiple slots
`children` is just a prop, so nothing stops you from passing several pieces of UI under different names.
Passing elements as props is also the simplest fix for prop drilling: instead of threading data through three layers, hand the finished element down from where the data already lives.
